About Milano, 2026

Drawn to culture, people and ideas, marketing was the natural fit.

Miguel is a Marketing Management student at IPAM, currently on Erasmus at Università IULM in Milan, where his coursework sits at the intersection of promotional marketing and luxury brand marketing.

Outside the classroom, he manages the full digital presence of a real client and stays close to the industry through events, certifications and people worth paying attention to, from a Yale course on financial markets to an inside look at the LVMH ecosystem.

Case study 04 · IULM Milano coursework

Haribo: Twin Snakes

A full go-to-market launch strategy for Twin Snakes, a two-sided sweet-and-sour gummy, built for the Italian market.

★ 30/30
Team roleStrategy & group project
CoursePromotional Marketing, IULM
MarketItaly

Haribo holds 97% brand awareness in Italy and leads the gummy category globally, but the fast-growing sour segment (+7% YoY) was still an open door. Twin Snakes, a two-headed gummy that's sweet on one side and sour on the other, was built to fill that gap without competing with Haribo's existing range.

The strategic bet: 89% of fruit gummy buyers don't have the product on their shopping list, so the campaign had to manufacture trial through surprise rather than through a shelf a shopper was already looking for.

Channel strategy
  • Priority 1, hypermarkets (Esselunga, Ipercoop, Carrefour, spanning 902 stores): the only channel with simultaneous control of the promo aisle and checkout, for maximum impulse visibility.
  • Priority 2, e-commerce (Amazon Italia, Esselungaacasa.it): the fastest-growing channel, allowing premium pricing without resistance.
  • Complementary: toy stores, travel retail (Malpensa & Linate) and cinema chains, each chosen for low competitive pressure and high indulgence-mode conversion.
  • Deliberately excluded: discount chains, where a price-only environment conflicts with the brand's perceived value.
A three-phase campaign
  • Launch (May/June): in-store promoters at checkout in hypermarkets, letting shoppers bite first and discover the second flavour after, filmed for Haribo Italy's social channels. Entry price held at €1.49.
  • Summer (July/Aug): a Gardaland Water Park partnership with two snake-shaped water slides (purple for sour, orange for sweet) turning the product into a physical attraction, with a branded stand at the exit.
  • Halloween (October): five simultaneous touchpoints across Milan under #TrickOrTaste, including limited-edition packaging, a branded tram and activations at UCI and The Space Cinema.
Projected KPIs
  • 15% trial rate in activated stores at launch; 50K+ Gardaland visitors exposed over the summer, with 500+ UGC posts tagged #TwinSnakes.
  • 90% pack sell-through target across the five Milan Halloween touchpoints by November 1st.
  • €485,000 total activation budget, projecting €1.8M in incremental year-one revenue at a 3.7x expected ROI, break-even at roughly 12 weeks post-launch.

Team project with Leonor Braga Fernandes, Donika Hyseni and Hannah Charlotte Kahn.

Case study 05 · IULM Milano coursework

Brunello Cucinelli: India Expansion

A market-entry strategy bringing Brunello Cucinelli's radical exclusivity to Mumbai, India's largest concentration of ultra-wealth.

★ 30/30
Team roleStrategy & group project
CourseLuxury Brand Marketing, IULM
MarketIndia

Brunello Cucinelli closed 2025 with 1.4 billion euros in revenue, up 10.1%, without ever discounting, chasing a mass audience, or appointing an external creative director. The brand's identity rests on nine consistent signatures, from its cashmere sourcing to a 47-year colour palette, and a stated strategic objective of pricing power over market share.

India was identified as the natural next frontier: the world's 6th-largest ultra-wealth population, with UHNWI numbers up 63% between 2021 and 2026, and a luxury market projected to grow from $10B to $25B by 2030. Mumbai alone holds 35.4% of India's ultra-rich, against zero existing Brunello Cucinelli presence.

Why Mumbai, why Jio World Plaza
  • Jio World Plaza is the only address housing 66 luxury brands including Louis Vuitton's largest India store, Dior, Cartier and Gucci, the sole location where Brunello Cucinelli plausibly belongs.
  • Giorgio Armani opened its Mumbai flagship at the same mall in 2025, its second India store after Delhi, setting a direct precedent.
  • Launch timed to Diwali, India's peak luxury consumption moment.
The capsule & the campaign
  • A two-piece India-exclusive capsule (a women's dress and a men's shirt), made in Italy using Indian banana fibre as a sustainable, symbolic material bridging Solomeo and Mumbai.
  • "Threads of Light": a week-long Diwali launch built around a press preview, a VIP opening, and a gratitude-lantern ritual where each guest's lit candle joined a growing central installation.
  • ATL support across out-of-home at Jio World Plaza, a dedicated digital strand, and a full-page placement in Vogue India's December issue.
Target clientele & KPIs
  • Four tiers, from UHNWI dynasties to emerging affluent prospects, anchored by personas like a third-generation Mumbai industrial heir and a returning NRI CFO based 400 metres from the mall.
  • Targets: 5 editorial features within 30 days of launch, 80% of VIP guests activated in CRM within a week, and a 90%+ sell-through on the exclusive Diwali capsule.

Team project with Leonor Braga Fernandes, Amir Isse Sagal, Claudia La Cara, Marina Pellizzari and Vittoria Schiavoni.

Case study 07 · IULM Milano coursework

Four Seasons: The Preparedness Manual

A crisis governance and risk-preparedness manual for Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, built around the group's real 2016-17 Sabre SynXis data breach.

★ 30/30
Team roleRisk evaluation & group project
CourseIssues and Crisis Management, IULM
FocusCrisis governance & escalation

Four Seasons manages, rather than owns, most of its properties, a model that ties its reputation to a dense web of guests, employees, owners and local authorities across 47 countries. The manual starts from that exposure and builds a full risk-to-response system around it, anchored by the brand's own 2016-17 Sabre SynXis breach, which exposed guest payment data through a third-party provider and led to a class action in the US.

Risk evaluation
  • Five macro-risk categories, from health and safety to cybersecurity and reputational threats, scored on likelihood and impact and plotted on a risk matrix to prioritise where preparedness investment should go first.
  • Health and safety and natural disasters land in the critical top zones; reputational and ethical risks stay high-impact despite lower likelihood, given the brand's positioning.
Crisis governance
  • A dual-level Crisis Management Team: a Corporate CMT for strategic oversight and reputational management, and a Property CMT for on-site, first-line response.
  • A three-tier escalation framework (Monitor, Respond, Crisis) with defined activation thresholds, a stakeholder notification matrix, and internal reporting channels including an anonymous ethics line and a corporate crisis desk for Level 3 events.
Response toolkit
  • Holding statement and press release templates for the food-safety and natural-disaster scenarios, built to go out within 30 minutes of a crisis breaking.
  • A spokesperson briefing sheet, social media response guidelines, a media monitoring framework, a stakeholder contact list and a crisis log, so every property responds with one coherent voice.

Team project with Martina Basile, Maddalena Bellino, Leonor Braga Fernandes, Jacopo Emilio Gorgoglione, Giulia Maestri, Giulia Maria Magro, Giada Panzeri and Gennaro Dante Sacco.

Case study 08 · IPAM Lisboa coursework

Academia Life Club: Product/Service Extension

Field-research-driven repositioning of a premium gym, moving it from "just another premium gym" to a performance and lifestyle destination.

★ 18/20
Team roleStrategy & field research
CourseGestão de Produto, IPAM Lisboa
OutcomePresented to the company as top project

In premium fitness markets, service quality alone no longer differentiates; what matters is who the offer is built for and in what context. Starting from that premise, the diagnosis combined internal analysis (specialised classes, integrated services, modern facilities, but an offer broad enough to blur into a generic "premium gym" perception) with external analysis (a mid-to-high-income audience that values personalisation, a strong sector growth outlook, but limited spontaneous foot traffic and unclear differentiation versus competitors).

Four problems were identified as the root of the club's stalled positioning: an external perception of being "just another premium gym," a lack of clear audience segmentation, digital communication that failed to differentiate, and visible aesthetic and branding inconsistencies.

Four strategic proposals
  • The environment as communication: fixing visible operational issues (cold female changing rooms, weak exterior signage), introducing premium product partnerships (Kérastase, Dyson) in the changing rooms, and a coherent neutral, sophisticated palette across common areas, digital communication and branding.
  • Professional Performance Programme: repositioning the club as a physical and mental performance centre for high-pressure professionals, with 60/90/120-day diagnostic-to-reassessment programmes segmented by professional profile, and partnerships with premium coworkings and boutique hotels.
  • Rising Stars: a disruptive talent programme supporting internal athletes and micro-influencers (bodybuilders, competitive athletes) with technical and competitive backing, turning their real training journeys into organic content and community connection.
  • Brand activations: invite-only lifestyle events co-created with premium partner brands, reinforcing the club's identity as an integrated wellbeing and urban lifestyle space.
Rollout & measurement
  • A three-phase implementation plan across all four proposals, from fixing operational basics and structuring programmes to scaling partnerships and building an annual premium events calendar.
  • KPIs set per proposal: NPS and perceived experience, new sign-ups and continuity in the performance programmes, organic growth and engagement for Rising Stars, and guest-to-member conversion and ROI for brand activations.

Team project with Leonor Braga Fernandes. Graded 18/20 and selected to be presented directly to the company as the best project of the course.

Case study 09 · IPAM Lisboa coursework

QPLAB: Strategic & Operational Communication Plan

A communication plan for a GMP-certified pharmaceutical testing lab, turning strong technical credibility into visibility, authority and qualified leads.

★ 18/20
Team roleStrategy & group project
CourseGestão da Comunicação, IPAM Lisboa
OutcomeBest project of the course, presented to the company

QPLAB is a GMP-certified analytical laboratory working 100% B2B with pharmaceutical manufacturers, regulators and medicinal cannabis producers, 70% of its activity based in Portugal and 30% international. The diagnosis found a company with a very strong technical base and a fragile communication one: no formal marketing department, no "About Us" narrative, weak SEO, and insufficient notoriety in priority international markets, despite deep expertise in quality control, GMP compliance and impurity testing.

Strategy 1: QPLAB Compliance Hub
  • A new website section combining an interactive GMP audit-readiness checklist (email-gated report as a qualified lead) with an SEO content hub targeting terms like "batch release" and "nitrosamine testing," where QPLAB was ranking far below competitors.
  • Prototyped live at qplab-readiness-hub.lovable.app.
Strategy 2: Institutional Story Hub
  • Reimagining the missing "About Us" as a Story Hub built on CIM and inbound principles: real success cases and case studies, content designed to be reused across newsletters, trade fairs and LinkedIn.
  • Benchmarked against Unilabs Pharma Solutions' own About Us and case-study structure. Prototyped at qplab-storyhub-showcase.lovable.app.
Strategy 3: Innovation Hub
  • Turning QPLAB's new facilities into an international communication asset: experiential flyers with QR-coded virtual tours, a Regulatory Open Day showcasing GMP practices, and presence at Pharma Congress, PharmaX Next and CPHI Worldwide in 2026.
Plan, budget & KPIs
  • A 12-month, SOSTAC-based rollout across all three hubs, with a €25,900 annual budget building from MVP development in Q1 to the Open Day and international fairs in Q4.
  • SMART targets: +30% organic visits, 500 qualified leads and +20% average time on site, tracked through technical-credibility, lead-generation, event and SEO KPIs.

Team project (Grupo 6) with Leonor Braga Fernandes. Graded 18/20 and selected as the best project of the course, presented directly to QPLAB.

Case study 06 · Client project

Connecta

A three-month launch strategy for Connecta, a hyperlocal marketplace connecting neighbourhood sellers, buyers and couriers, built to win on trust and locality rather than speed.

RoleLaunch strategy, presented to the founders
SectorHyperlocal marketplace
MarketLisboa

The starting question was what Too Good To Go did differently from Glovo or Uber Eats. Glovo sells convenience: customers hide that they use it, and the brand stays invisible inside the product. Too Good To Go sells a cause: customers display that they use it, because the content it generates is real impact, not a generic discount. 90% of Too Good To Go's growth is organic, because the app gives its customers something they actually want to show off. Connecta's launch strategy is built on the same logic.

Five strategic directions, combined over 3 months
  • A. The Local Countdown: instead of an infinite Amazon-style catalogue, sellers post what only exists today, right there, turning every product into a deadline rather than a listing.
  • B. Neighbourhood Ambassadors: 3 to 5 local micro-creators (500 to 5,000 followers) become the visible face of the launch, paid on performance rather than reach.
  • C. Anti-Giant Movement: positioning Connecta not as another app but as a stance, your neighbourhood doesn't need Amazon, reinforced by a "Bought Local" seal sellers use on their own channels.
  • D. Disruptive Physical Presence: a one-day pop-up market featuring only Connecta sellers, so the first impression is a real encounter, not another icon on a phone.
  • E. Emerging Creators (Gen Z): a five-minute store setup for young people sitting on an untested product idea, recruited through personal networks at close to zero acquisition cost.
Seller incentives
  • A first-sales guarantee: Connecta buys back unsold stock at sale price for the first 15 days, up to a small cap, removing the fear of selling nothing.
  • Zero commission, not just low commission, for the first 30 days, plus a free professional photoshoot for early sellers.
  • A weekly seller leaderboard competing for pride and visibility, not only discounts.
Four audiences, one map
  • Buyers, sellers, couriers and emerging creators, each mapped with distinct motivations and a distinct channel to reach them, from door-to-door recruitment to WhatsApp-only onboarding for less tech-comfortable sellers.
  • Positioned deliberately local and niche on a 2×2 against Too Good To Go, Glovo/Uber Eats and Amazon, the one quadrant none of them occupy.
Risks flagged upfront
  • Strategic: network effects are slow to start, and a working local model is copyable by larger platforms once proven.
  • Legal & regulatory: food safety liability, VAT handling for small sellers, and data protection obligations from real-time location.
  • Financial: low commission means volume takes time to compensate, so early cash flow needs close monitoring.

Closed with four open decisions for the founders: the final entry category, the specific Lisbon neighbourhood for launch, the real order of magnitude for budget, and the founders' comfort with the positioning itself, deliberately left for them to decide rather than buried inside a slide.

Writing & analysis

Original thinking on brand and luxury strategy, first published on LinkedIn.

Original research · originally published on LinkedIn

The Desire-Accessibility Paradox

How K-shaped growth is splitting the luxury market in two, and what six houses reveal about which side they're building for.

Luxury demand today is polarising. Growth is concentrating among high-value clients, while many aspirational consumers are being priced out of the category altogether: a K-shaped split rather than a rising tide.

The underlying question every house has to answer is whether it is building visible cultural desire or deeper client relationships, rather than trying to optimise for both at once. High prices, on their own, aren't what creates exclusivity. Disciplined pricing, scarcity and trusted relationships do more of that work than sticker shock ever could.

Illustrative reading of the framework, adapted from the original six-house analysis.

Key takeaways
  • The luxury market is increasingly polarised, with growth concentrated among high-value clients while many aspirational consumers are priced out.
  • Brands need to choose whether they're building visible cultural desire or deeper client relationships, rather than optimising for both at once.
  • High prices aren't the key driver of exclusivity. Disciplined pricing, scarcity and trusted relationships build stronger long-term demand.

Full article, with sources & dataset
Field analysis · originally published on LinkedIn

5 luxury brands. 5 different strategies.

One week in Milan, during Fuorisalone 2026, spent reading what each brand's level of effort reveals about where it actually stands in the luxury hierarchy.

During Fuorisalone 2026, activations from Gucci, Moncler, Valentino, Audemars Piguet and Hermès were all reachable within the same week in Milan. What stood out wasn't the installations themselves, it was how each brand's level of effort revealed exactly where it stands in the luxury hierarchy.

Five brands, five readings
  • Valentino went all in: immersive spaces, bold aesthetics, generous gifting. A brand actively building cultural relevance.
  • Moncler put a giant inflatable octopus on a rooftop: disruptive, impossible to ignore, designed to be shared. Audience expansion without losing cool.
  • Gucci told its origin story through monumental tapestries: a brand reconnecting with its own identity after years of creative reinvention.
  • Audemars Piguet kept it small and intentional: a window installation of cogs and gears built out into the street, turning horology into architecture. You only earned the gift if you solved their challenge first. Scarcity by design, even when it's free.
  • Hermès did nothing: no activation, no gifting, just product, displayed in silence.

And somehow, that silence was the most powerful statement of all. The higher a brand sits in luxury, the less it needs to convince anyone. The brand doesn't come to you, you come to the brand. That's not passivity. That's the ultimate brand positioning.
